Question three. What do the HTTP status code classes mean? The first digit tells the story. Two hundreds succeed: two hundred OK, two oh one created, two oh four no content. Three hundreds redirect. Four hundreds blame the client, and five hundreds the server. The right code lets a client handle a failure in code, instead of parsing an error message. Question four. Four oh one versus four oh three, what is the difference? Four oh one, unauthorized, is really about authentication: the request has no valid credentials, and the response carries a challenge header saying how to authenticate. Four oh three, forbidden, means the server understood the request and refuses it. The credentials may be fine; they just aren't enough, and logging in again won't necessarily help. The follow-up: some APIs answer four oh four instead, on purpose, so a stranger can't learn that the resource exists.

Question five. What is idempotency, and why does it matter for APIs? An idempotent operation has the same result whether it runs once or many times. It matters because networks fail. A client that times out can't tell whether its request arrived, so it retries. Here's a payment of fifty dollars, sent with POST, which HTTP doesn't make idempotent. The first attempt is charged but its response is lost, and the client retries twice. Three charges: a hundred and fifty dollars. The fix is an idempotency key: a unique ID the client generates once and sends with every attempt. The server stores it with the payment. Each retry finds the key, inserts nothing, and gets the original payment back. Three requests, one charge. What makes it safe is a unique constraint on the key: even two retries racing each other can't both get in, because the database refuses the second.
